In this tutorial, we implement OmniParseBench , Datalab’s open benchmark for document parsers, which grades a parser’s output with 16,288 small pass-or-fail tests across 2,937 pages, from scanned forms and handwriting to arXiv math and dense tables. Rather than trust the leaderboard, we rebuild it from the verdicts Datalab released for 27 parsers, after feeding the scorer a hand-made page to see which mistakes flip a verdict. We then measure ranking certainty, slice it by document type, test whether the two models the card names as helping build tests behave differently on tests a model corrected, and run Tesseract and Indra OCR ourselves on a 50-page sample. Along the way, we find that the top two parsers are statistically tied, the leader changes on most slices, and one launch figure doesn’t match the released files. A one-letter typo, a lost minus sign, a different symbol in an equation, swapped headings and a mislabelled block each flip exactly one test to fail, with a reason attached. The controls still pass : capitals, a dropped thousands separator and dfrac in place of frac, because text is folded and equations are compared after KaTeX renders them. The headline is the mean of the text, tables and layout pass rates with unsupported tests left out, so a parser that cannot return layout blocks, such as Tesseract, gets no headline at all. All 108 entries in the card’s table match its one-decimal values. The recomputation also exposes a near tie at the top: Datalab accurate and Gemini 3.8 Flash both round to 92.9, 0.024 points apart, and pooling every test instead of averaging families puts Gemini first. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser def per_document(df, systems, groups): """For each system: an array (documents x groups x [passes, scored tests]); `groups` maps a name to a row mask.""" docs = {d: i for i, d in enumerate(sorted(df.document.unique()))} s = df[df.result != "unsupported"] out = {} for name in systems: g = s[s.system == name] arr = np.zeros((len(docs), len(groups), 2)) for k, mask in enumerate(groups.values()): sel = g[mask(g)] d = sel.document.map(docs).to_numpy() arr[:, k, 0] = np.bincount(d, weights=(sel.result == "pass").to_numpy(), minlength=len(docs)) arr[:, k, 1] = np.bincount(d, minlength=len(docs)) out[name] = arr return out, len(docs) def resample(n_docs, B, seed): """B bootstrap resamples of the documents, each as a count per document.""" rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) return np.stack([np.bincount(rng.integers(0, n_docs, n_docs), minlength=n_docs) for _ in range(B)]).astype(float) @section("5. How sure is the order at the top? A document-level bootstrap") def bootstrap_step(): top = list(TABLE.headline.nlargest(6).index) families = {f: (lambda g, f=f: g.family == f) for f in ("text", "tables", "layout")} arrs, n_docs = per_document(VERDICTS[VERDICTS.system.isin(top)], top, families) W = resample(n_docs, 2000, seed=20261022) head = {} for s in top: tot = np.tensordot(W, arrs[s], axes=([1], [0])) # resamples x families x [passes, tests] head[s] = 100 * (tot[..., 0] / tot[..., 1]).mean(axis=1) point = {s: 100 * (arrs[s].sum(0)[:, 0] / arrs[s].sum(0)[:, 1]).mean() for s in top} print(f"2,000 resamples of {n_docs:,} documents; a document's tests stay together\n") print(f"{'parser':22s} {'headline':>9s} {'95% interval':>15s} {'gap to ' + top[0]:>26s} {'resamples where it leads':>24s}") leader = np.argmax(np.stack([head[x] for x in top]), axis=0) for s in top: lo, hi = np.percentile(head[s], [2.5, 97.5]) d = head[top[0]] - head[s] gap = "" if s == top[0] else f"{point[top[0]] - point[s]:+.2f} [{np.percentile(d, 2.5):+.2f}, {np.percentile(d, 97.5):+.2f}]" print(f"{s:22s} {point[s]:9.2f} {lo:6.2f} - {hi:6.2f} {gap:>26s} {100 * np.mean(leader == top.index(s)):23.1f}%") d = head[top[0]] - head[top[1]] lo, hi = np.percentile(d, [2.5, 97.5]) claim(f"{top[0]} and {top[1]} cannot be told apart (the 95% interval of their gap includes zero)", lo < 0 < hi) return f"{top[0]} vs {top[1]}: {point[top[0]] - point[top[1]]:+.2f} points, 95% interval [{lo:+.2f}, {hi:+.2f}]" bootstrap_step() A gap that small raises the question of how much of the order is noise. T ests on one document tend to pass or fail together, so we resample documents rather than tests : each of 2,000 draws picks 2,343 documents with replacement and recomputes every headline from per-document pass counts with one matrix product. The gap between the top two runs ranges from about -0.9 to +0.9 points, and each leads in roughly half the draws, so the honest reading is a tie. Datalab balanced, 1.35 points behind the leader, is clearly separated from it, and so is every parser below. We r ecompute the headline on handwriting, rotated pages, tables, single scripts , and other slices with the same family-mean rule, after an assertion confirms that the rule reproduces the official headlines on the full set. The overall leader comes first on only three of thirteen slices. Gemini 3.8 Flash leads on handwriting, math, and forms; Claude Sonnet 5.5 on rotated pages; and Mistral OCR on Greek. It also lists what we did not run here: the hosted parsers that need paid keys, the GPU models, latency and cost, and the full set of 2,937 pages. In conclusion, OmniParseBench is a benchmark we can audit end to end: the scorer is open code that calls no model, the verdicts are released, and every entry on the card can be rebuilt from them. The top two parsers are statistically tied, pooling tests instead of families changes the order, and a different parser comes first on handwriting, rotated pages, tables and several scripts. The two models named on the card fall less far than the others on tests a model corrected, which we report as a flag rather than proof. Tesseract’s published verdicts reproduced exactly on our sample, while Indra OCR’s agreed on 92% of tests. The practical lesson is to slice the benchmark to our own documents, report intervals, and pin every version. Check out the Notebook and Repo . All credit goes to the researcher of this project.
